JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

The Irrepressible Scouts. It was a chastening if not humiliating dis- covery for the Latchford Cadet Corps when they realised that a couple of audacious Boy Scouts of the Ist Latchford Troop had succeeded in carrying off their colours from the very centre of their camp at Bradshaw Farm; and a con- solatory word or two may not be amiss. When a young reporter attending the old Voltinteer encampments of the Victorian era, I had ex- perience of a smart stroke of the character now referred to, though on a more ambitious and extensive scale. There were Yorkshire artillery in camp at Bare, and others stationed at a point about ten miles away, and one night the latter stole in upon the former, and,. easily eluding the guard, cut the cords of every tent on the field, dropped the canvas on the unconscioui occupants, and reached their own quarters again without being identified!

Rush bearing. " Critic " laments the decay of "Ye oldg rushbearing " at Lymm. :The most artistil rushcart I ever saw was at Rochdale. The occasion was the celebration of the jubilee of incorporation of the borough, and among the representative's in the procession was a picturesque group of Morris dancers drawing, or " bearing " this perfect and memorable rush- =rt. Both there and at Bacup I have repeatedly seen parties of Morris dancers, and have greatly enjoyed their performances. On the Decline.

Excepting at Knutsford and a few other places, the May Day festivities on& so general and so robust may likewise be said to be, in a galloping consumption. I was at Otley a little while, and in the centre of the town was a fine Maypole. Once it came to grief, but was promptly restored by the enthusiastic inhabi- tants. A later generation showed strange iii- difference to all that it meant to their fathers-. When I was at Halifax the outlying village of Warley had its Maypole and it yearly festival, but with the disappearance of the one several years ago the other ceased, and Warley has forfeited the distinction of which it was for- merly so proud.

" Wireless" 100 Years Ago. This reminds me, oddly enough, that a high hill overlooking Halifax is, surmounted by a beacon the original of which, at the period of the " Boney " scare, formed a link in the chain whereby news of an invasion was (or were, As Sir Walter Scott is always careful correctly to render it) •to be flashed across the country. Thus there was a sort of wireless telegraphy in use or available long before Marconi was born. Mourning Dress.

In a "Woman's World" paragraph on " The influenCe of colours" " Marjorie " cites an authority as deprecating the wearing of black for hygienic reasons, and strongly commending the use of white .materials. I fear it is a counsel of perfection for these latitudes. In China, of course, white is mourning wear. I read with interest that in the 15th vol. of the Journal of the Anthropological Institute Professor Frazer raises several points in relation to this question of mourning dress that have not been definitely settled. It is clear, he says, that mourning; garb was intended to be something quite dis- tinctive from, "if not the reverse of, ordinary costume, but its exact purpose seems still to be under diScussion. It has been suggested that it was meant as a disguise in order to deceive the ghost of the dead. It appears that all kinds of Spirits are easily deceived, and it seems plain that protection , was required from the spirits of the dead, but from various examples it is by no means clear that that pro- tection took the form of disguise. Other sug- gestions are that mourning garb and customs were intended as a return to more primitive conditions as a means of expressing the union with the dead. The mourner was supposed to partake to some extent of the conditions of the dead, especially during the arduous journey of the ghost to its ultimate home. The real in- tention (adds Mr. E. S. Hartland, to whose in- teresting paper read some time ago before the Anthropological Section of the British Associa- tion I am now indebted) seems more likely to have been an expression of sorrow and abase- Ment, so as to deprecate the malice of a spirit which was naturally annoyed at finding itself disembodied.

div.head: USEFUL GIRL.
div.p: A USEFUL GIRL.

A sixteen-year-old girl is acting as Govern- ment blacksmith at the village of Pollington, near Silaith. She is Miss Alice Bateman, the only daughter of the village blacksmith, and has replaced her father's workman, who has joined the Army. She shoes horses, repairs all kinds of agricultural implements, and every. day helps her father to make thirty horse-shoes for the War Office. From 5.30 a.m. to 2 p.m. she is engaged on Government work. Then she tackles the needs of the local farmers in the way of repairs and horseshoeing.

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.

WHERE THE CYCLE SCORES. In these days of petrol restrictions the cycle is becoming, and rightly so, even more popular than ever. Many whom I know have already put aside their cars and motor cycles and have returned to their first love. This is excellent in many ways. It is excellent because it reduces the demand for petrol; it is equally excellent because cycling is far and away more health-giving than motoring. There is no surer waiy of retaining one's health than by exercise in the open air. And there is no open- air exercise so good as cycling; not only for the young and strong, but also for the middle aged. It is often imagined that cycling is only suitable for the young and energetic. Never was there a greater mistake. So long as the rider is willini to take things easily and not overdb himself, there is no reason at all why the man of sixty should not in- dulge in the pastime. If he will be content to " potter " about on his machine he will derive enormous benefit. . The great advantage that will accrue to him is that gentle exercise may be taken in the open-air, and, as a greater distance can be covered than if he walks, fresh districts may be visited each time he mounts his machine. In cycling the weight of the body is taken off the legs, and this renders the strain less than if a walk is taken. The power 'required to propel a cycle is not sufficient• to lay an excessive strain on the heart or lungs; hence very few are prevented from joining the ranks of the cycling community. Wherever muscular effort is allowed at all cycling is less fatiguing than any other method of taking exercise.

div.head: TO CURE A LEAKY TAP.
div.p: TO CURE A LEAKY TAP.

As most motor cyclists know, the remedS, to cure leak in the petrol tap or elsewhere is to grind in the tap. But this is an operation requiring great core, otherwise the result is that matters will be much worse than they were before. Tap grind- ing is a very tricky business, and requires the most scrupulous care. But it can be done, of, course, and this is the way to do it: First take the tap to pieces and thoroughly clean all the parts. Then smear the parts to be ground in with. the slightest smear of the finest crocus powder obtain- able and proceed with the grinding. Five or six turns will usually be enough, for a start anyway, and the tap should be tested after this. Remember that the grinding has to be done with a simul- taneous revolving pushing motion. One wofd more: before resorting to grinding, see if you can- not cure the leak by driving the tap further home with a light hammer.

SWORN IN.
Warrington Volunteer Training Corps.

Prior t 9 the " swearing-in " ceremony which had been announced to take place on Sunday at noon, about 142 members of the Warrington Volunteer Training Corp paraded at the Parish Church, under their commandant, Captain W. Peter Rylands. His Worship- the Mayor (Alderman P. Peacock) was present.

The service at the church was conducted by the Rev. S. G. Stanton, who, during his ser- mon, referred to the spirit of patriotisiu which was spread abroad at the present time, said it was Such that had prompted these volunteers to do whatever lay within their power for their country in her hour of need. Patriotism was the bond which united the individual to his country and led him to identify himself with the spirit of the nation, and to place his services at the disposal of his fellow-countrymen. That spirit had been strik_ ingkly emphasised in the present crisis, and had inspired the people of this land to heroic acts of self-sacrifice and service. But, with all our national pride, we must remember that we be- longed to a still bigger family, to which we were united by the ties of humanity and by the universal Fatherhood of God—the great family of mankind throughout the world. The spirit or cenduct of any nation, which .was but a part of the whole of mankind, must be judged not from a purely national standpoint, but by its effect upon the human race as a whole: It was possible for a nation to be a menace to the rest of the world, as we believed was the case to=day. For nations as for individuals there were two ideals—a right and a wrong. The right ideal was to bring its special gifts to the service of Mankind, and its keynote was service, while the wrong ideal was to develop its own powers and resources, regardless of the welfare of any sec- tion of humanity other than itself. Our national patriotism must be the means to a greater end—the service of humanity. Mr. F. A. Frost, officer commanding Grap- penhall Detachment of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment, was present. At the conclusion Of the service the men smartly formed up—a number being in, uniform =and marched to the front of the Town Hall, where the " swearing-in " took place. The Commandant himself first took the oath. With hat doffed, and a Bible in his right hand he repeated after the Mayor, the following words, which composed the oath :-=" I do sincerely promise and swear that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to His Majesty King, George V., and that I will faithfully serve His' Majesty in Great Britain for the defence of the same against all his enemies and opposers whatsoever, according to the conditionalof my service." The men afterwards came forward in groups of ten or twelve and went through the same ceremony. ' Eighty-five of the whole' num- ber on parade were sworn, when the supply of enrolment forms was exhausted. As soon as a further supply is available the 'remaining mem- bers can be sworn-in, either before a magistrate or by an officer who has himself taken the oath of allegiance.
At the conclusion of the " swearing-in " the -men stood to attention, said "God Save the King," and the parade was dismissed. •

div.head: WORKING MEN SUPPORT THE INFIRMARY.
div.p: WORKING MEN SUPPORT THE INFIRMARY.
Eighth Musical Festival.

The Union Jack was hoisted over the Town Hall on Sunday afternoon. This announced that the grand concert organised by the Work- ing Men's Infirmary Committee in aid of War- rington Infirmary and Navy Day was being held in the. Park. Otherwise—had the weather been unfavourable—the event would have taken place in the Parr Hall. The Work- ing Men's Committee (of which his Worship the Mayor is president), must have felt delighted with the success of their eighth annual festival. Hundreds of people trooped into Bank Park be- fore three o'clock, and in a very short space of time there was scarcely a vacant place on the seats arranged in rows before a large improvised platform. The audience included quite a large number of wounded soldiers.

The presence of the fine band of the 2nd Battalion Pringe of Wales' Volunteers (South Lancashire Reginaent),'by kind permission of Lieutenant-Colonel J. L. Vaughan, proved ln enormous attraction. Their rendering of the various orchestral items on the programme was conspicuously meritorious, and the conductor, Mr. R. E. Cahill, had to bow his acknowledg- ments to the vigorous applause at the close of each selection. In their first contribution'he overture from " Saul " (Bazzini), their com- petence was not severely tested, as with the , exception of the closing passages the work is rather uninteresting; but their handling 'of portions of Mascagni's gem, " Cavalleria Rusticana," is worthy of all praise. A selec- tion from the works of Sullivan led one rather to expect some of the many popular favourites, but Winterbottom seems to have wandered more into the byways of ,his composer's genius in search of melodic beauties. One passage strongly brought to mind the ghostly measure in the , opera " Ruddigore." But the band were un- questionably heard at their best in Lab's 'Norwegian Rhapsody. Here was a composition 'entirely to their taste—full of light and shade, buoyant music and orchestral surprises, it was excellently performed. ' Mr. J. IT. Draper and Mr. Arthur C. Pearce were the soloists, and they combated very suc- 'cessfully with the difficulties attending al fresco singing. Mr. Draper rendered "The Trum- peter" (Dix) with extremely good effect, and Mr. Pearce wits heard to advantage in that im- pressive declamatory 'passage from "Elijah," "Is not His word like a fire?" Both vocalists were most harmonious in the duet, "Watch- man, what of the night?" Mr. Payton accompanied. The first item on the programme was the hymn "0 God, otir help in ages past," and the last but one, "Abide with me." Both these well-known tunes were played by the band and the audience sang the words. The effect was unusually sweet and impressive. During an interval Mr. W. Peter Rylands, at the request of His Worship the Mayor, asked those present to signify their appreciation of the kindness of the band, the vocalists and accompanist in coming to the concert. Needl.4ss to say this was heartily done.

div.head: EVENING CONCERT IN THE HIPPODROME.
div.p: EVENING CONCERT IN THE HIPPODROME.

For the purposes of an evening concert the Hippodrome was kindly lent by Mr. F. Macnaghten, the members of the permanent staff co-operating in the arrangements under the guidance of the courteous manager, Mr. Will A. Jackson. In the favourable conditions afforded on the Hippodrome stage the Bandsmen of the South Lancashire Regiment, 'under Mr. R. E. Cahill's conductorship, did justice to themselves and added further sprays to the laurels they have won from Warrington audiences. The fine overture "Maximilian Robespierre" (Litolff) and the " Finlandia" of Sibelius were the two most important items in the programme, and those therefore which tested most strongly the all-round, qualifications of the performers. From this ordeal they emerged with high credit, an admirable resonance and sense of massiveness pervading all they did in these two numbers. Characterised, as they are, by broad masses of harmony, the works mentioned lose little in effectiveness in adaptation for wind instruments alone. Indeed, in the clash of battle depicted in the overture, and in the enunciation of the virile phrases of the Tone Poem, there would seem to be greater possi- bilities, in the military band, of that realistic interpretation of the music upon which com- plete success depends. -

Some fine individual executive work was shown during the evening, that in the tenor horn and euphonium 'sections being especially worthy of praise. In the realm of pure melody one had a rare treat in the Traviata selections and in the collocation of Gounod's works, in both of which opportunities for solo playing by particular instrumentalists were splendidly taken advantage of. In this connection special mention should be ?made of the cornet solo rendering of Liddle's moving song "Abide with me."

Miss Nellie Anderton's two songs, " The Lost Chord" and "A Song of Thanksgiving," served to show that. that talented singer's voice has gained in range and roundness of tone since she was last heard in the Hippodrome. To both songs she imparted an intensity of feeling and an impressiveness which were as admirable as they were artistic and appro- priate. The band parts of Sullivan's great song, which had, we understand, been specially scored by Mr. Cahill, added not a little, by their restraint and unobtrusiveness, to the climax. of Miss Anderton's highly successful rendering of it. The bass songs by Mr. E. Pearce were not particularly interesting. "Arm, arm, ye brave," and "Why do the nati.ons?" sung to a pianoforte accompaniment were felt to be something of an anti-climax, notwithstanding the fact that the vocalist's fine voice and robust 'style were brought to bear in a brave endeavour to make them tell. It seemed a pity that, with so fine a body of instrumentalists at call, these two big excerpts from Handers works should not have been sung with the more adequate background of this military orchestra. To some extent, therefore, sympathy should be extended to Mr. W. H. Payton in the some- what thankless task he undertook of accom- panying on the pianoforte these extracts from the oratorios.

div.head: Proud To Be Mayor.
div.p: Proud To Be Mayor.

During an interval the Mayor (Alderman. Peter Peacock) took the opportunity, as presi- dent of the Working Men's Infirmary Com- mittee, of thanking Lieutenant-Colonel J. L. Vaughan and the officers of the regiment for permission given to the members of the band to give their services once more. It was s., plea- sure to find that their playing was quite up to the usual high standard to which they always attained. They in Warrington seemed almost to own the band—(laughter)—for every time their services were asked for they were given willingly, and they always gave satisfaction. He particularly desired to thank Miss Anderton and Mr. Pearce for their services; the directors of the Hippodrome, and Mr. Jackson, the manager, for allowing the use of the building. The Hippodrome was used more for these charitable purposes than any other institution in Warringtim, and it was, therefore, the duty' of the public to patronise that house whenever they could on other occasions. (Applause.) Over £2,000 had been obtained by the Navy, Day effort—(applause)—and now he was grati- fied to find that the public were so handsomely supporting the Infirmary as well as the Navy Day movement. "The longer I am Mayor," added Alderman Peacock, the more I am pleased to belong to a town like Warrington. When I was first appointed Mayor, I was dis- appointed with the appeal I 'made for support to good objects. I thought the public were rather stingy, and I told them so, but the war, as it had gone on, has opened the hearts of all to give as well as to work. I am proud to he Mayor of a town like Warrington." (Ap- plause.)

The coat-fiock scored its first success in serge and alpaca, and undoubtedly the latter material appears at its best in this garment, smarter in fact than when used for coats and skirts. But the summer has brought a demand for the coolest of clothing, and even the lightest alpaca is sometimes unbearable. The coat-frock, however, has not been laid aside for autumn' wear; it has been adapted for all tempera trims, and is proving as fascinating and -comfortable in cotton voile and casement cloth, as in winter fabrics. In these materials it is just the tiling for motoring, and takes the place of the coat which is too heavy in the hottest weather, even for the seaside and country. In shantung and taffetas the coat frock is admirable, and some of the new models have revers of the pelerine variety, and very deep cuffs. Cotton fabrics are being made into simple walking suits, whose distinction lies in the henistitching finish that is given to fronts and basques. If made at tor:he the hem- stitching takes some time, but the effect is worth the trouble. Barley-meat Scones. \

Bring to a boil a , pint of new milk .and stir into it barley-meal until you have, a rather thick paste, add salt required and turn the dough on to a dish to get cold. Spread it then with more barley-meal and knead till the dough is smooth. Roll out very thin, stamp out in rounds. Bake each side a few minutes on the girdle. True barley-meal scones are made without any raising material whatever. The dough is simply rolled out as thin as a wafer previous to, putting it on the girdle. Barley-meal scones may be made in a similar way to white scones, using a teaspoon- ful of cream of tartar and half a teaspoonful of carbonate of soda to each pound of barley- meal. When done in this latter way. the dough is usually rolled out thin to about the size of the girdle and baked whole—not in any way cut.

Rub a tablespoonful of butter, lard, or drip- ping into half a pound of barley-meal and quarter of a pound of white flour, then mix in a teaspoonful of cream of tartar, one of pounded sugar, and a little salt. Dissolve a teaspoonful of carbonate of soda in a little buttermilk, add as much more milk as is re- quired.,to make a soft dough. Turn it out lon board, roll out to thickness of quarter of an inch. Dip cutter or tumbler frequently in flour and stamp out in rounds, bake one side on hot girdle a few minutes, turn and bake the other side. In baking white scones, it is customary on taking them from the girdle to pile them while hot one on the other in order to keep them moist with the condensed steam. But in the case of barley-meal scones, each must be kept apart until thoroughly cold.

The Order of St. George and Catherine the Great.

It is interesting to note that the Russian Order of St. George, of which so Much is heard of just now, was instituted by a woman—Catherine the Great. She was both polite and far- seeing, and recognised the importance of a high military standard in her army, which she desired to bind closely to herself. She there- fore founded the Order in 1769, as a mark of distinction and reward for zeal and duty shown by soldiers. In order, that its value might be more appreciated, she bestowed it but rarely, and it ranks to-day with our Victoria Cross. Like the latter, the medal is very simple: a Maltese Cross of silver, with a figure in the centre of the warrior saint, and the dragon he conquered. There were four grades of the Order originally, but a fifth class was created later, and now men in the navy as well as the army, are eligible for this degree of the reward of merit. War Souvenirs and Mascots.

Many soldiers in• the French Army are skilled workers in the ,precious metals, and in their leisure moments they have made all sorts of curious souvenirs of the war, from the metal taken from enemy , arms and 'accoutrements. The debris of -some of the priceless old stained glass, once the glory of the windows in French and Belgian cathedrals, have been used as jewels, and set to form the loveliest rings and pieces of jewellery. The purples, blues, and rose tints of these fragments of glass are unsur- passed in beauty, and doubtless, in a few years' time, this war jewellery will Command a high price for public and private collections. Mascots and souvenirs were never more in evidence than they are to-day. Some are ex- ceedingly quaint, and a few are costly. Quite a new idea is the initial wristlet, a parting gift that appeals to the sentimental. The husband or lover has two of his initials made in enamel and diamonds, or any other precious stones he may prefer, ‘and‘ these are attached to a black moire ribbon and worn as a bracelet by the wife or fiancee. A favourite present to the soldier is a dozen or so of lucky handkerchiefs, with a cat, dog, parrot or other animal embroidered in one corner.

div.head: WAR-TIME VEGETABLES.
div.p: WAR-TIME VEGETABLES.
Latchford Garden Society Encourage Home-Grown Food.
AID FOR RED CROSS.

It was a happy idea on the part of the officials of the Latchford Garden Society to devote the proceeds of their show this year to- wards the funds of the Raddon Court Red Cross , Hospital, for the show, held in the grounds of the hospital on Saturday afternoon was a brilliant success, no less a sum than £5O being handed over to the hospital, while further amounts have yet to be received. Combined with the show was a grand gal, which included concerts, special competitioAs, and amuse- ment stalls, which comprised "all the fun of .the fair." The show itself was a great improvement on last year's display, the fine selection of flowers being a feature. The mixed vases of flowers arid the farm produce. were elwellent; while the wounded soldiers' special vegetable exhibitions, as one of the judges remarked, "required a good deal of judging."
- The opening -ceremony was performed by Colonel Moggridge, the Rev. G. C. Briggs (president of the society) presiding.
GROW YOUR OWN VEGETABLES.

The Chairman, reviewing the objects of the society, said! one of them since the outbreak of war had \been to _encourage the people to exer- cise economy by cultivating potatoes and vege- tables as much- as possible. The society had been hard hit' by the ,war, like many other societies, but 'their work was being kept up. By giving the whole of the proceeds of the show to the hospital' the society were giving up' an important source of income, but they could not be helping a better cause than they were doing that day. (Applause.) In declaring the show open, Camel Mog- gridge expressed thanks to the society for giving the proceeds to the hospital, which was a worthy object.

That was a most welcome sug- gestion, and came at a very appropriate time, for they were just about to instal six new beds for extra accommodation. (Applause.) She thanked the Mayor for attending. " Can Hardly Realise How Welcome It Is Out Here."

Private James David Scott, of the South Lancashires, son of Mr. David Scott, 61, Kim- berley-street, and foreman over the wire boys at Longford Wire Works, has sent the follow- ing letter home:— - "Sunday, August 20th, 1916.—Many thanks for 'Examiner' just received, after waiting eight days. You can hardly realise how wel- come it is out her* When I receive it the boys say `ls that he "Examiner"?' and when I answer ' Yes'—well, there is a rush for news. I am very pleased to say I am going on quite all right, and am quite well. I hope all at home are the same.
Away From The Firing Line.

"We are now in a nice, quiet village, miles away from the firing line. You see, our divi- sion have gone down on rest (which they deserve), so you can go to sleep to-night with an easy mind, knowing that I am out of range of the German guns. It will please you to know that our battalion have been praised by the General for their good work; and he said that irre are a fine lot of fellows and are worthy of praise. All the 'boys' are in the 'pink,' and are always looking forward for letters and papers which they receive from home. Thanks For Tobacco.
"In this letter I wish to thank all those who contribute to the local Tobacco Fund, for the 'boys' think a lot of the ` they receive from 'Blighty.'
"Well, i must now close, wishing the good old 'Examiner' and the Editor every success in the future. With the fondest love."
Private Scott, who is-onl3----nlneic:en years of age, enlisted last November, went to France May 3rd, and was in the thick of the fray, on July 6th.

div.head: MISSED THE TIDE.
div.p: MISSED THE TIDE.

Mr. LLOYD GEoili.E has taken up LORD KITCHENER'S' role as analyst of the military situation, and he plays this part as well as the many others he has undertaken. In his survey this week he sounded both a note of confidence and a note of warning, but the chief point of his finding is that Germany has missed the Aide—and Germany knows it. "Surveying the whole situation,," he declared, "in the light of existing facts, and upon the advice of those who are far more competent to...express an opinion than I am, I have no hesitation in saying that all this country and the Allies have got to do is to march together steadily, work together loyally as they have done in the past, and then victory, assured victory, will rest in their hands." Going into details he pointed out that in two months we had wrested the initiative from the enemy, who had been compelled to take guns and munitions from Verdun, and concentrate them on our front. In this way; the pressure on Verdun has been relieved, and the enemy has been prevented from detaching part of his forces to support the Austrians against General BRITSILOPF. It is true that Germany's armies are probably as numerous and their , equipment as formidable as ever; but this is not the case with Germany's allies, chiefly I, because we have been able to concentrate such great forces that we have held Germany while the Russians afe dealing with some of her allies, and so. he was able to say, "We have captured the ridge, we can See at any rate the course of the campaign, and I think, in the dim distance, we can see the end." We shall need; Mr. LLOYD GEORGE' re- minded the House in his note of warning, more men, more munitions, more guns, and all the courage And endurance of our race. There is no fear of any slackening in any department in this country—the 'terrible casualty lists we are publishing, locally and generally, call for stern vengeance, which will be meted out in due season and at all costs.

Mr. CHURCHILL, dealing with the question of food supplies, urged that the Government should boldly put food ,supplies "on a war basis." If restriction were necessary, it should be achieved by the issue of bread and meat tickets, or by the institution of meatless days. He demanded that the Government should take over the entire control of ship- ping. The latter part of Mr. CHURCHILL'S speech consisted of a somewhat mystifying appeal to the Government not to bq deterred by financial considerations from buying "the necessary supplies" of munitions from Am-erica for the use of Russia. Mr. CHURCHILL apparently did not intend to sug- gest, that the Government really needed any such admonition—" he knew," he said, " that the Government had made great exertions in that r9spect "—but the temptation to lecture the Government seemed to be irresistible.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, 1916.
GOSSIP.
Corporal Tombs, the Warrington V.C., met Private Procter, the Liverpool V.C., on Mon- day when the latter was being given a civic reception in Liverpool. The two shook hands and were loudly cheered.

V.C.'s are not so numerous as Private Procter thinks they ought to be, for, he declared, if his Cross had been split in a hundred pieces to be distributed among his comrades "it would' be only what was right."

I had the privilege this week of a few moments' conversation with Heesom, the Warrington boy D.C.M. He did grim work when lie won his distinction. and he was liter- ally in a tight corner when' he was buried last month by a shell explosion—but lie is all smiles, as becomes a British "Tommy."

The Frost family' are, like most families, doing their duty and suffering to the full. Lieutenant Robert Frost, of the Liverpool Regiment, who figures in the casualties this week, is a cousin of Mr. F. A. Frost.

I recall a conversation I had with Mr. F. A. Frost quite a fortnight before the present advance began. He had had letters from a Parisian friend giving the most precise infor- mation upon the military situation._

This friend enclosed letters from officers at the Front, saying that Verdun would neV-e-r fall; ,that the Germans were losing men so quickly that it was sad to se& the slaughter— even of Bosehes; and that the British on the French left were just ready to show the Germans that they could fight as well on land as they had shown, off Jutland, that they could fight at sea.
I eould not give this prediction at the time, but the Censor will have no objection now the thing has ben dom..

Among those eligible for service are men called up under the Military Service Act and time-expired Territorials. div.p: M. CHARLES DUKES.
Question And Answer In The
House Of Commons.

Mr. Forster has replied in Parliamentary papers to Mr. Snowden, who asked if he was aware that Charles Dukes, organising secretary of the General Labourers' Union, was called upon to report himself at 8 a.m. on Friday, August 18th, and that he was arrested by the police at 9 the same morning; if he is aware that the warrant was prepared and all the arrangements made to arrest Mr. Dukes before the expiration of the time for repo, ',mg, him- self; and, seeing that Mr. Dukes was one of the trade union officials for whose exemption the General Labourers' Union applied on the grounds of his indispensability, he would take action to order his release for his trade union and public work.'
"Charles Dukes has had every latitude shown to him," says Mr. Forster, who in reply hi- stances the many appeals made between Apzil 28th and August Bth, and adds—

"This man had received careful considera- tion by the War Office and Loctil Government Board, but it was decided that the decision of the Tribunal ought not to be interfered with. I am not aware of the circuinstances mentioned in the earlier part of the question, but as Mr. Dukes could properly have been required to report for service before August 18th, no fur- ther steps can be taken by the War Office."

Compensation in Lieu of Notice. A claim for compensation for dismissal in lieu of notice was heard by Mr. T. J. Ridgway at Warrington Munitions Court on Monday. The complainant was Arthur Meakin, of, 3, Scott- street, employed formerly by a local firm as labourer.

Mr. Arthur E. Seabury. National Union General Workers, conducted the man's case, in the absence of Mr. Charles Dukes. It was ex- plained that on July 17th Meakin was obliged to stop work, and procured a medical certificate showing that he was unfit to resume. He came back on the 31st July, when he was told that his place had been filled. He was given his cer- tificate, but had been out of work until August 15th. With bonus and overtime he used to earn £2 a week. He had been with the firm for six- teen years. The manager of the firm said that was the first time he saw the certificate produced. When the man stayed out and did not let them have a notification in writing, his place was filled up. • The case was allowed to stand for the attend- ance of the foreman to whom Meakin said he showed the doctor's certificate on the afternoon of July 17th. The foreman subsequently attended and stated that the certificate was not produced until the man returned. The Court Awarded one week's wages, 275, as compensation.

div.p: WARRINGTON OFFICERS FOR THE
FLYING CORPS.
Captains 0. Lyon Whittle And A. Skinner Win Their " Wings " And Go To France.

There is a good deal of .satisfaction in know- ing that Warringto-n is now represented in the Royal. Flying Corps by two officers, who, until .recently, were members of the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment._
In the, "London Gazette" of last Saturday appeared the following :
ROYAL PLYING CORPS. Military Wing.—The following appointments are made:—

Flying Officars.—Lieutenant (temporary Captain) 0. L. Whittle', South Lancashire Regiment, Territorial Force. Lieutenant (temporary Captain) A. Skinner, South Lancashire Regiment, Terri- torial Force.

These two gallant Territorial officers have thus been transferred from our local, battalion to the Military Section of the Flying Corps. As a matter of fact, both are now on duty in France. They have been close friends since their early school days, almost inseparable, and fate or

fortune has kept them together throughout the war. Wherever one went the other by mere chance followed, and although they were this month sent abroad on different dates and to different places, fortune has brought them to- getheg again in France. They met by mere accident, for in the last letter Captain Skinner sent home was a request for information as to the •whereabouts of 'Captain Whittle. Needless to add, the transfer of. Captain Skinner to another squadron was soon arranged by a friendly and sympathetic C.O. I; oth officers joined the Territorial§ long before the war; they went to the Front as lieutenants in February, 1915, with their battalion; and both ,were wounded and invalided home. They were promoted captains while On active service in France. Tiring of the monotony of ,training troops at home, and anxious for more active service, they applied for transfer to the R.F.C. early in January this year. After completinr, their training in several • places in England', they successfully passed their examinations and won their "wings" last month.

div.head: MILITARY MEDAL.
div.p: MILITARY MEDAL.
Private S. Emery Delivers A Message
. Though Voimded.

About six weeks ao we reported that Private Stephen Emery, of the Machine, Gun Section, Royal Welsh Fusiliers, Son of Mr. and Mrs. S. Emery, 3, Dalton-bank, had been wounded in the back by ki machine gun bullet and brought. to hospital at Brighton. It now appears that Private Emery received this wound while- per- forming a .verr.brave deed, for which- he has been awarded the Military Medal. His name appeared in a list of aWards,in a supplement to the "London Gazette." The good news was

conveyed to his parent' on Sunday morning in the following letter from Lieut. J. H. Oliver Thompson:— " I have great pleasure in informing you that for, his gallantry in the recent offensive your son, Private S. Emery, has been awarded the Military Medal. He received the medal for the following incident: During the action he was carrying ‘messages from 'gun to gun, exposed to shell and machine gun fire, and, although being

wounded, succeeded in getting his message de- livered before he would leave his post to go to the dressing station." During his stay in hospital Private Emery has been visited by his mother, but, , with a modesty characteristic of the: British , soldier, has mentioned nothing about the deed which gained him the distinction. - Private Emery, who is 22 years of age, enlisted in September, 1914, and has been at the Front over twelve months. Information has reached Mrs. Haddock, 7, Ernest-street, of the death in action of her hus- band, Private Joseph Haddock, of the South Lanes. Regiment. Private, Haddock, who served in the Army for five years prior to' the war, was formerly employed by Mr. Broadhurst, contractor, Wilderspool-road. He was educated at Stretton School. He re-enlisted over twelve months ago, and had been at the Front for six months. Captain Dickson and the other officers wish to express how keenly we feel his loss. He was a fine soldier and never complained, even under trying conditions. Please accept our heartfelt sympathy in this time of your sorrow, and always remember that your husband died doing his duty and his bit."

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
PRODUCTIVE
Ak REMARKABLY
SEASON.

The " Times " sums up the position thus: With the exception of wheat, we are in the enjoyment of a remarkably productive season. This fact is greatly enhanced by the extraordin- ary abundance of hay and grass. Neither is it a matter for surprise that in a season eminently adapted for the growth of herbage of all kinds wheat prospects should have suffered to a certain degree. The season is extremely late, especially in alf northern and high districts; but lateness is due to earlier low temperatures and excess of moisture, boat of which con- ditions favour grass. The increase in tempera- ture during July to a degree almost tropical, together with an unusual amount of moisture in the soil, stimulated growth in almost every county. We must not take into account so much of exceptions as of the general results of the season, and our reports show that from the extreme north to the extreme south we have secured record crops of hay, and are in the enjoyment of a record ,growth of srass. The tm portance of this accession of general productive- ness is likely to place the present season on a high pedestAl in comparison with ajarge num- ber of its predecessors. A big grass crop natur- ally involves some spoilt hay; and an undue growth of weeds. Botjt. are subjects of com- plaint, but the last month of fine weather has • enabled by far the greater part of the meadow hay to be secured in excellent condition, and at the same time has improved the prospects of all the arable land crops.

div.head: LANCASHIRE HARVEST.
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE HARVEST.

Early this week a general start was made with harvesting on South and West Lancashire farms, where, despite the buffeting and heavy rains of last week's thunderstorms, the corn has stood remarkably well, making the work of the self-binders and harvesters compara- tively light. Hundreds of machines are at work, and the crops 'are above the average, with exceptional- length of straw.- The opening quotation of grain, when threshed, is likely to surpass all previous records for the past 60 or 70 years. div.head: TOMATOES SCALDED.
div.p: TOMATOES SCALDED.

A correspondent sends me some tomatoes on which may be found several yellow spots, the cause of which he is anxious to know. The fruits sent are what is known as scalded, which is caused when in the morning the ffuits are damp with moisture because the house has been shut up close, and the sun coming out brightly has scalded them before they were dry. Scalding, too, is often caused by the

stupid plan a cutting away the foliage. Rich food is given in excess to the plants, with the 'result that there being no foliage to absorb, such food, it is forced into the fruits, causing Had flavour, spot, and scalding. We do not denude other plants of their leaves in the same way as one often sees tomatoes treated, and when this severe removal of the foliage is car- ried out little wonder is it that scalding ensues. The smooth :varieties of tomato are more liable to scalding than the corrugated sorts, probably due to the skin being more Sensitive.

Hearing Unusual sounds coming from One of our leading establishments on Wednesday even- ing, I decided to enter, and, to ray delight, I found a dinner party in full swing, the centra seats of honour being occupied by two well- known local soldiers, who were surrounded by a host .of pals. I was immediately made a member of the party and did ample justice to the lamb and green peas that our host and hostess, Mr. and Mrs. A. Sutton, had so ably provided. For some considerable time the object of the dinner Was kept from me, but, I ascertained from one of the distinguished guests that the dinner had been given by a fei'v youths of Lymm in honour of a visit of two of their old friends, who had been fighting the Huns for the last two years, Privates Percy CIOPre and J. Gilberts.

div.head: Pies From Preston.
div.p: Pies From Preston.

Although the dinner had been kept a pro- found secret, news of it had evidently leaked out, for on Wednesday morning the host was the recipient of a parcel .bearing the Preston postmark and containing three tempting pies and three black puddings, and a note which bore the abrupt Message, "Hope you have a grand evening; from two , little girls at Pres- ton." The host. entered with ' this parcel, placed the pies on the table, announced their place of origin, and /left us to our fate. The " carving " disclosed the fact that the pies did

div.head: PRIVATE J. GILBERTS
div.p: PRIVATE J. GILBERTS
lot contain beef, but A selection of little toys. Ahen we realised how cleverly we had been waxed by two mere girls, we immediately took off our hats to the "two little girls from Preston."
H a rmon y.

Dinner concluded, we set about arranging a small concert, and • with the help of Mr. A. Pilkington with a set of bones, and Mr. Wm. Bradburn with the irresistible tin whistle; we provided a very able orchestra. .• Songs and recitations were then rendered by Mr. H. Leather, who, with a rich baritone voice, opened the proceedings with that familiar, Scotch song "Annie Laurie." Mr. John Con- naughton rendered several whistling solos in masterly style, and the distinguished guests rendered patriotic melodies as sung in the dug- outs of Flanders. Mr. Ben Jolley was re- sponsible for the humour. Gramophone selec- tions were also rendered by Mr. William Jolley. While the fun was at its highest "The Examiner" man called the distinguished guests into an ante-room and there got them to relate their experiences of the Great Push. When I announced what these two heroes . were about to do the fun automatically ceased and, the guests were as eager to hear as a little child is when its mother relates it a fairy story to get it to sleep.
Saturday Night, June 30th.

"It was Friday night," commenced one of the two heroes, '" the 30th of June, and the work of the day being done we sat in our billets, getting the time over ,by singing and larking, when suddenly the order rapped the air in clear, shrill tones, 'Fall in for rum issue,' which plainly 'meant that there was 'something doing.' We fell in, in fighting 'order, and were then joined by our late Captain and Company Commander, Captain G. W. C. Hartley, who, it is interesting to know, has been appointed 'Town Major' over a well- known French town; and although it was im- possible for him to come into action 'with us, he accompanied us well on, our way. The' dis- tame from where we fell in to 'the trenches was a matter of about five miles, and that 'five miles took us well over three hours to accomplish. , Shortly after we began to move the order came along !March at ease,' which meant. that we could sing, shout, and do any- thing we liked as long as we kept in the ranks, and, needless to say, our little friends, the 'Woodbines,' were jolly soon brought into action. Although shells were flying in every direction, we made the best of things, and all the men were in the best of spirits; in fact, they might have been going to a similar 'd o' as we have had to-night, so jovial and eager were they to get at it. We have heard it said that we did not know what we were going up for, but we did. 'Tommy's' sense of humour even ;in the greatest danger is a striking fea- ture in this war. You can even hear jokes being passed when a shell just misses its mark and fails to hit its object. Marching along, singing. laughing and joking, we would suddenly hear someone shout 'Hey up, lads; here's mimmi-whaffer [meaning a shell]; get down!' But, no! .We' knew what we had. to do. and the sooner we reached our destination (the trenches) the better; so we stuck it and kept on going."
Arrival At Trenches.

"We arrived," said hero No. 2. "at the sup- port trehches about 2 a.m. on the Saturday morn_ ing, the Ist of July, and immediately. took up our position; then the officer came round and told us to take things as comfortable as pos- sible, for in a few hours we would no doubt need all our energy. All morning the shelling continued, and we were the recipients of presents from the Kaiser from almost every quarter, but. pleasing to say, with little result. _ _ _ _

"During this time the British and, French artillery had been getting ready, and at 5 a.m. they got into action. Never was such a row heard before. div.head: CORPORAL HARRY THOMASON.
div.p: CORPORAL HARRY THOMASON.
AAT,ounded In Right Shoulder.

Corporal Harry Thomason, Rush Green, has been wounded in the right shoulder and is at present undergoing treatment at the Western Hospital, Tootal-road, Manchester. He enlisted soon after the outbreak of war, ,and had been in France about seven months, and was a`member of a machine gun section. Prior to the war he was a member of the National Reserves and was an old member of the 3rd -1- oi. Battalion Cheshire. Regiment, which was disbanded. During his service with this regiment he was looked upon as one of the finest shots in the battalion, anil held the company cup., He is also the proud . possessor of several 'other honours for shooting. He took a keen ,interest in football, and was connected with the Lymm A.F.C. He is 28 years old, and was educated and worshipped at Oughtrington, and is highly respected in this neighbourhood. His wife
visited him in the• Manchester hospital last Monday and found him doing very well and very comfortable. Prior to the war he was emPloyed at the M.S.C. Co.'s brickworks at Statham.

Constable's Smart Capture.—At the Lymm Sessions House on Tuesday, before Messrs. S. W. Gould. and F. Lockyer, a Manchester man was charged with deserting from the 21st Reserve Battalion Lancashire Fusiliers, now stationed at Press Heath Camp, Whitchurch. Evidence of arrest was given by Acting-Sergeant Griffiths, who stated that he called at the house where prisoner was lodging at Massey Brook. Prisoner admitted that he had been in the Army, and produced a discharge certificate dated September sth, 1915. He denied that he had ever been in the Army since that date. He also denied being in possession of any uniform. Witness took him to the Police Station, and told him that he was going to, brink the man who gave him a ride in a cart from Warrington to Thelwall, he being then in uniform, and prisoner admitted being a deserter. His uniform and kitbag were after- wards found in a hedge at The!wall Brook.—The magistrates warmly commended the sergeant on his smart capture, and awarded him 15s. Pris- oner was ordered to be detained in custedy and handed over to the military authorities.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wounded Soldiers Entertained.—Owing to the kindness of the members of the Padgate Tennis and Bowling Club, about 40 wounded soldiers from the Lord Derby Hospital, Winwick, were entertained to tea on Thursday afternoon. Dur ing the interval before and after tea some cf the visitors joined in a hearty game of tennis, whilst others joined in a game of bowls. The visitors were brought from the hospital in a 'bus, which was lent by Mr. Connor, of War- rington, and the return, journey to the hospital was make about seven o'clock.

Boy Scouts.—About twelve members of the 2nd Troop of Padgate Scouts, in charge of the Assistant Scoutmaster (Mr. W. J. Bate), had a very enjoyable route march on Saturday after- noon last. Leaving headquarters at 2.40, they proceeded via Fearnhead and Croft to Cul- cheth. Visits were also made to Kenyon to view the college and also the Culcheth Cottage Heme 4. Tea was served in the outskirts of the village, after • which the return journey was made via Newchurch, Risley and Fearnhead, arriving back at 8 p.m. Whilst passing through Croft the boys were invited by Mr. John Hough- ton to inspect a Prussian Guard's helmet, which had been sent home from the firing line by his son, Private John Houghton, of the Manchester Regiment. It is also interesting to record that Private Houghton has been awarded the Military Medal for bravery in the field, and the boys were shown the ribbon for the medal which had been sent over by him in a letter the same morning.

Fred Woods, Sankey Bridges, a well-known Penketh Tannery worker, paid a visit home last Saturday week for a few days' leave, but was notified the following morning to return im- mediately to his depot on the East Coast. His military career counts from September, 1914, when he joined the Army Service Corps. He found himself in France after six weeks' train- ing, and remained there until last Christmas, when he was invalided home.

Cycling Accident.—A very serious cycling accident took place on Friday night of last week to Norman, eldest son of Mr. Joseph Lee, Warrington-road, Penketh. Whilst returning home from delivering a message his machine skidded in some thick dust, bringing him down. He threw out his leg to reduce the shock of falling, and it gave way under him. Be- lieving at first that he had badly sprained his ankle, he lay down, hoping for the pain to go off. The Rev. H. T. Dixon, passing by, found him in a helpless condition and commandeered a bath chair, by which means he was removed to his, home, were Dr. Murray was soon in 'at- tendance. It was found that the right shin bone was broken, but owing to the swelling of the ankle it was impossible to state how far that part had been injured until the %Wowing day, when a further inspection provrm rt to be also broken. The limb has been set and the patient is• progressing favourably.

Private J. J. Starkey Wounded.—Private J. J. Starkey, of the South Lancashire Regiment, was wounded on August 4th in the head and right arm with shrapnel, but his mother, who lives at Brook House, Grappenhall:road, cind visited her son recently in Stockport, states that he is in excellent .spirits.' He was ,in a trench on the British Front when a, shell burst on top of _a portion of the trench and partially buried the soldiers in it. Musician Killed By Explosion

A large number of friends in Stockton Heath were shocked last week to learn of the death of Corporal. Harry Frederick Patton, son 'of Mr. Henry Parton, Stockton Mount, London- 'road.' Mr. Parton learned the sad fact from his son's commanding officer, who wrote :—" I very much regret to inforra you that your son yesterday (August 14th) met with an aecident caused by the bursting of a shell, and I am sorry to 'say the injuries caused by the ex- plosion proved fatal. The burial took place with such honours as were possible under active service conditions. I would ask you to accept my sincere sympathy and that of the unit under my command." The young non-corn. was only ip years of age, and joined the A.S.C. He acted as dis- patch rider. He was in France over twelve months, and had expected to get home on leave on August 10th. He was educated in the People's College and assisted his father in the business in Stockton Heath. He attended the Parish Church of St. Thomas', and was very I Popular. He was an adept musician, and took la keen interest in boxing. He had travelled to America and Australia.

div.p: POULTRY NOTES.
CHANCE OF FOOD.

A sudden change in the fdod, too, often acts ad- versely on the egg production. So long as the birds are laying well, change merely for the sake of change must be deprecated; on the other hand, if they are laying badly, a change of diet can do no harm, and may do good. Soft food is quite unnece.s- sary at this season, and, as maize is more tinsuit-, able in summer than in winter, there is not much variety left; a mixture of oats and tail wheat is about the best food they can have. If a change is thought necessary, a little barley may be given, but not for long, as it has some of the bad effects of maize. Buckwheat is a useful change grain, bat difficult to obtain good at a reasonable price; in-, ferior buckwheat is not suitable for fowls. It is worth while pointing out that one drawback of having the laying hens hatched about the same time is that they all moult about the same time; this is very inconvenient--we want some hens W moult early and some late. In selecting pullets for stock this fact should be borne in mind.—" Farm- and Home."

div.head: TO IMPROVE A CHICKEN HOUSE.
div.p: TO IMPROVE A CHICKEN HOUSE.

Many chicken hOnses fail in that they are made of insufficiently thick material. Boarding not more than tin. is sometimes used, which is much too thin to maintain anything approaching an equable temperature inside the house. A good Plan with a house of this description is to tar it on the outside. and while the' tar is wet to lay on some sheets of very thick brown paper or unbleached calico. Two more coats of tar should then be applied. It will be found that such an arrange—, meat 'adds greatly to the/coolness of the house in I summer and to its warmth in ,winter. Whitewash- ing the roof is also a2.very golod plan, making the interior much cooler. To 4 gallons of lime and water 11b. of soap should be added, which causes the preparation to adhere closely for several months.

div.head: FEEDING IN HOT WEATHER.
div.p: FEEDING IN HOT WEATHER.

Certain poultry foods there are which should be avoided during hot weather, since they contain too generous a proportion of carbohydrates and fat, the elements which generate animal heat. Partfeo- larly is maize an unsuitable food at such a time; fo also is barley, but to a lesser degree. Both have the effect of producing fat and of maintaining the bodily temperature too high. There are really onlY two occasions when maize ought to be employed, and these are during cold, weather and to sitting hens; at no other time is its use recommended. Even during the winter it requires to be sparingly' employed, and it should never be in a greater proportion than about one-fourth of the whole mix- ture. The most suitable meals for hot weather are ground oats, middlings and bran, and the hest grains are wheat, oats, and, when easily procurable, buckwheat. When the weather is extremely hot' cold mash may be provided first thing in the mor.n- ing, and an excellent mixture is two parts mid- dlings, one part ground 'oats, one part bran, andi, half a part 000ked lean meat.—" Farm and Home;

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS.

Colonel Arthur Stanleigh and Judge Lamar Stanleigh, cousins, of Virginia, are bitter enemies ever the. possession of the Diamond from the Sky, a massive jewel heirloom found centuries ago in a fallen meteor. Colonel Stanleigh, when a daughter is born, buys the male heir of a gipsy king, that he may keep the jewel. He plans to rear Esther. the girl, in secrecy. Esther and The Diamond from the Sky are stolen by Hagar, the gipsy mother. Years later Hagar returns Esther and the diamond, but of the old group only Dr. Lee is living. Blair Stanleigh kills Dr. Lee and steals the jewel. Then Blair Stanleigh and Arthur Stan- leigh, the false heir, fight a duel. Arthur, thinking he has killed his cousin, flees in a racing motor car. In his mad flight the machine goes over a river bank, and that night the moon shines on a body floating down the stream. Arthur is found by Esther and Hagar and nursed to health. Hagar tells him his real identity. Arthur swears to make *himself worthy of Esther and leaves, taking the diamond, and meets Blair Stanleigh. Blair takes him to a great ball, where they meet Vivian Marston, a New York belle, wearing the diamt.nd. Hagar is there, too, telling fortunes. Vivian has just seated herself when a brawny forearm. clutches The Diamond from the Sky. A greater confusion than that caused by the loss of the diamond arises when the Sheriff of Fairfax arrives 'at the ball and demands the arrest of Arthur Stanleigh. He escapes, partly through the efforts of Hagar, and later finds work and refuge as a farm hand. Luke Lovell drops the diamond into a mail-bag. The fen, clings by its Clasp to a rent in the bag, and is afterwards found by Quabba, the hunchback °rgan-grinder. He does not retain it long; Clar- ence, his monkey, drops it an owl's nest. Arthur, working on a farm as "John Powell," masks him- and goes to the Fairfax tournament, where he wins the hirhest honour. He is betrayed by Blair Stanleigh, and amid great confusion the young- Virginians fight ,to bar Arthur's escape without avail. Hagar, holding proofs of Blair Stanleigh's guilt, is brutally attacked by the-young man and her mind destroyed. The diamond finds its way to a Chinese opium den, whence Blair steals it. Vivian marries him, and they escape from Tom Blake in a train which robbers board and take the diamond, with other jewels and money. Pursued by a Sheriff's posse, the train robbers lose the diamond and treasure, the latter being found by 'John Powell." Blair presses his attentions upon Esther, who spurns his professed love. Arthur Stanleigh has become rich by .the purchase of a gushing oil well, and through Tom Blake purchases Stanleigh Hall. Luke Lovell secures the diamond from an Indian squaw, but loses it though the treachery of his partner, who knocks him into the sea. ,

missed the thoughts of Vivian and the marriage from her mind. It was Brair's mother, also, who constantly inspired him with thoughts of Esther. The very day the letter had come from Vivian to Blair his mother received a letter from Mr. Hunter, the legal adviser of the Stanleighs, who, as referee in bankruptcy, had charge of Stanleigh Hall when it went to, Detective Blake as highest bidder for some unknown client. The lawyer had written:

"Der Mrs. Stanleigh,—ln reply to your inquiry, The Diamond from the Sky is legally the property of any sole heir of the late Colonel Stanleigh, whether a son or daughter, irrespective of family tradition regarding it and the Earldom of Stan- leigh."

Mrs. Stanleigh had shown this letter to her son, and revoiced er beliefs and suspicions. "I believe this girl, Esther Harding, is the real and only heir to all that Colonel Stanleigh died possessed of. We have no proof I knew, but I believe Hagar Harding had such proof, and now the girl has it. I believe, too, thilt she carries it with her. If this girl is the rightful heir of Stanleigh, the clAmond is hers, and if Arthur Stanleigh is an impostor the Earldoin in England is yours. Had Colonel Stan- leigh not been so bitter in his feul with your father, or your father not so bitter with him, Colonel Stanleigh would have been too proud not to have accepted the family tradition and turned over the diamond to you as the rightful heir in case the child he expected was a girl. "We are bound to silence owing to your rash and reckless acts. We must make the best of the situation. If a stranger has bought Stanleigh Hall the sale is not legal, and if this girl Esther is the real Stanleigh the estates must be restored to her, and the diamond rightfully belongs to her. What will she care for the family traditions if it ever comes about that she is able to prove, or desires to prove, her claim? Doubtless she is keeping silent out of regard for Arthur Stanleigh. "There is a simple thing to do, Blair. You must marry this girl. Then you will have a clear claim to the title, and you will also possess Stan- leigh Hall and the diamond. No matter where the diamond may be, it must ultimately come to light. You can then choose whether you will surrender it to the Blooms as the price of their silence, as is now arranged, or buy them off with the wealth that comes to you as the 'Earl of Stan- leigh.", •

To get Esther and the diamond by such means, not to speak of the Stanleigh earldom in England, appealed to Blair. The thought of Vivian fighting for her rights as the consort of an earl appealed to Blair's cynical sense of humour.- He .'as, in- deed, a worthy scion of a line that traced itself from the desperate and ,unseiupulous Sir Arthur Stanleigh who found, the famous diamond. ' Blair meekly fell in with his mother's proposals and prepared to return to Richmond, where Tom Blake, the detective, was receiving orders from two clients. Arthur Stanleigh wired: "Spare no expense in finding Esther. Keep me advised." Abe Bloom was the other client. He continued to chafe under the loss of the diamond, and said to the detective: " I may be a gambler, but I do not trust Vivian Marston. I want you to go west and find the diamond." The same" day Mrs. Burton Randolph was sur- prised to see Blair arrive. He professed to be anxious for Esther's welfare. "Esther is on some foolish quest. We must save her from the conse- quences of her folly." "What do you know of Esther?" asked the lady. "She left hero some time ago." "I know that very well, but just now I saw her leave that hunchback organ-grinder and go into Riverview Sanatorium. We'll go there and see what is happening,”

Quite innocently Mrs. Randolph fell into the trap and accompanied the young man to the institution. Esther had found Hagar gradually improving, and in her joy she listened to Mrs. Randolph's pleading to stay with her until her mother was sufficiently well to be taken away. Through one of his aides Tom Blake heard that both Blair and Esther had arrived in Richmond. Carrying out Arthur's instructions to take care of the girl he gave his helper money to secretly give the girl. "Sent by Arthur to be used as neces- sary," was the note with the money. Before leaving with Mrs. Randolph, Esther whispered a few words to Quabba, and that worthy walked away, followed by Blair, who' in turn was followed by Blake's young man. Al; the corner of the' street Quabba was knocked down by a tramcar. Blair was among the first to come to his assistance, and heard him give the address of his lodgings, where he asked to be taken instead of to a hospital. The quick brain of Blair saw a way of testing his mother's belief that Esther carried the Stanleigh secret with her. He wrote a note as a stranger, stating that Quabba had been injured and would like her to come and see him. Seeking a messenger he handed the note to Blake's assistant, and that astute young man hur- ried to his employer with the message. His suspi- cions aroused, Blake disguised himself and took the note to the girl, who immediately set out to find Quabba. Scenting danger, Blake followea. Meanwhile Blair had obtained, entrance to Quabba's room, and had bound and gagged the gipsy before Esther's light slep was heard at the door. As the girl stepped in she was confronted, by Blair, wearing a mask. "Give' me whatever document you have," de- manded he.

"What do you mean? I have no document." "Yes you have, and unless you hand it over I shall take it," said the desperate man, seizing the girl. She struggled gamely, but would have fared ill at the hands of the violent man if Tom Blake had not rushed into the room and attacked Blair. A battle royal ensued and things were going badly for the detective, strong man though he was, until Esther released Quabba, and that irate individual took a hand in the fight. Out through the door on to the stairs the fight waged until the banisters gave way beneath the strain, and Blair fell to the floor below, bleedina and stunned. Esther, with 131ako and Quabba, ran down the stairs, and, lifting the mask of the insensible man, recognised Blair Stanleigh as their assailant. "You recognise him? Well, we must get away before the police come." _

With the boom of the surf sounding in his ears, Panting and chilled to the bone, Luke Lovell pulled himself up on the beach. The fight in the boat was like a hideous nightmare. Somewhere beneath the waters .of the bay the body of his treacherous Partner was lying. From the pier he could hear scurrying feet. Men had heard the awful shriek of the doomed man as the death /he had intended for Luke had claimed him. And the diamond? Again the Stanleigh "charm against harm 'S had brought death to the hands that would have won it with violence. Luke had no time for further reflection. If he wished tc• remain a free man, neither the police nor the owner of the boat now floating in the bay must find him. The bewildered Man concluded, not without reason, that• the dia- mond was a very devil's fetish when in the hands of those who coveted it without right of _possession.

In whatever light the gipsy regarded The Dia- mond from the Sky. Vivian Marston held no scruples. Despite the troubles it had already brought her, she was anxiously in search of the 'onderful jewel. It might be a talisman of woe for some people, but not for her. Vivian had had many ups and downs in her adventurous career, but the balance, as she proudly said one day to a friend, was most decidedly on the credit side, and it would not be her fault if the diamond remained out of her possession. .

But the presence of Blair Stanleigh was essential to success. After all, he was not a bad sort, and, supposing illegitimate means failed to _secure the diamond, there was always the possibility of Blair becoming heir to the treasure. Beyond that there was the earldom to be considered, and, above all things. Vivian felt that she would like to be a countess and hold her head up among the aristo- cracy of England. There was no false pride about the young woman, at least she said not, and if she could not wear the coronet of a countess with distinction her schooling in various grades of society did not count for much. So, being essential to her schemes. Vivian wrote to Blair: "Los Angeles, " September 4th.

"My Dear Boy,—Am sorry we parted in anger about the diamond. Arthur Stanleigh, under the name of 'John Powell,' has struck it rich in oil here. You had better join me, and let bygones be bygones.—Lovingly, VIVIAN." Away in Fairfax Blair received the letter. He crushed it and wondered. fin the presence of Vivian, Blair was as a man kunder a toxic spell. He remembered with bitterne4 her light and scorn- ful dismissal of him. She had married him for The Diamond from the Sky. He had risked his life for it and her. Yet when the train robbers had despoiled them of the great gem she had thrown him aside and mocked him. Now she needed him and sent for him. Blair was young, full-blooded, unscrupulous, and passionate. The sweet and beautiful development of Esther's char- acter and person, now that he was relieved of the intoxicating presence of Vivian, had roused An Blair's breast a longing for Esther that he thought Was love.

Was it true, as Abe Bloom, the gambler, had hinted—and Abe Bloom had known the lady of old—that Vivian Marston possessed perhaps several' husband,, and that her marriage, secret and hasty, to Blair in Richmond previous to their flight with the diamond was null and void? STORIES OF THE WAR.
WHY PARCELS FROM HOME ARE APPRECIATED.
Private J. A. Brownbill (a former employe of the Warrington Co-operative Society), who is serving in France with the K.O.R.L. Regiment, Writing to Mr. Morris, an employe of the Society, says:—

"Just a few lines to thank you one and all for the most excellent parcel of foodstuffs. It could not have come at a more opportune time, for we are in thee trenches, and, of course, it is rather difficult to get food supplies down. Everything here is very dear, especially to buy from 'the -French people. Our commanding officer and chaplain have opened a canteen for our boys, to enable them to get things at cheaper prices, and I have been placed in charge of it. These are some of, the prices of tinned fruits at the B.E.F. div.head: BOMBARDMENT IN THE lITIENCHES.
div.p: BOMBARDMENT IN THE lITIENCHES.
Lively Scenes Described By Private
Tomlinson.
Private Harold Tomlinson, writing to his wife, 37, Fothergill-street, gives the following experiences of a bombardment in the trenches: He formerly worked at Mr. Jackson's, pawn- broker :

"In a .farmyard somewhere in France, July 22nd, 1916. . "I am now going to describe what a bom- bardment bf the trenches is like. lam lucky to be alive to-day. On Thursday night we sent a party of men out in front to put some barbed wire up, and they were seen and heard by the Germans. I was on 'trench duty with my pal, we were taking it in turns, I slept 'while he was on duty. It was about 1.30 a.m. when, all the trouble commenced. I was asleep, but was suddenly awakened, or rather half- a.wakened, liy the voices of men of the• barbed wire party returning in a hurry and scattering about. Shells began to pour on us from the German lines and I found I was alone, nobody anywhere near me. I dared not move or I would have been killed almost certain. So there I lay with shells dropping in front of ,ine, behind me, and to my right and left, on they came, 'whiz bang," whiz, whiz, bang.' It was terrible, high explosives as well. I crouched up in the corner of my shelter, putting two packs on top of me, a haversack and my overcoat to std the splinteKs of the bursting shells. I knew there was a safer dug-out fur- ther up the trench, but I daren't move, as I was facing all the shells. Two shells struck the next shelter to mine and smothered itie with dirt. I was expecting to be hit any minute, and I was quite ready, but I prayed and prayed and clung to my rosary. This went on for_half an hour; then the Germans began to cool down, sending shells every two or three seconds, so I took the opportunity and dashed up the trench into the small dug-out, which was empty, then another shower of shells came, lasting about 20 minutes, but I was safer now. What a sight it was. I will never forget it as long as I live. It seems the Germans thought we were going to attack them, and that is why they bom- barded us.

div.head: Marvellous Luck.
div.p: Marvellous Luck.

"All the fellows were surprised to see me alive. They knew I was in my ,shelter, and one chap came searching for my body. The Com- manding Officer said I had a marvellous bit of luck. Two shells fell just three yards to my left. A wall (clay) separated them - from me. While I lay there my tongue became parched; then my lips, and I nearly choked. The fellows told me it was shell shock. In the morning, when daylight came, I looked where I had slept and found several pieces of shell splinters. All the other fellows had got away in time, but I was asleep. They were awake, having been working. My chum said he was coming to wake me up, but dare not go any farther, so he turned back and took shelter with the others. We came out of the trenches on Thurs- day and were shelled while on the road. We had to walk down a communication trench that was two miles long. We marched about six miles to a village and rested for the night. I received your parcel there. Oh, I danced with joy; so did my chum. How well it was packed up! I was pleased with it. We had a splendid tea, and it' aould never have come at a more apprilpriate time. The• cream, biscuits and everything else were all that could be desired. As soon' as I saw it I said 'God bless her.' My- chuth noticed the quality of the stuff and re- marked bow nice they were. We marched off to this place in the morning; it's about 12 or 14 miles. It was a pitiful march, men began to drop out, falling flat on the dusty roads, the sun was scorching; it is the worst march I have ever had. I finished up the last three miles holding on to a pack mule, it nearly dragged me along. Everybody Was the same. all saying that they had never done a march like.that be- fore. We are now in a barn."

div.head: LAYERING CARNATIONS.
div.p: LAYERING CARNATIONS.

More carnations are probably lost from neg- lect to layer thein it the proper time than from all other causes put together. Early layering should be the rule, as shoots.put'down now should, if all goes well, be 1411 rooted by the first fortnight in September, when they an be planted out, or left on the parent plant till later, as they will gain in strength and take no harm/ A wet season is not conducive to the free rooting of carnations. If the soil is friable, and in a medium condition as regards moisture, very little water is needed after it is seen that the shoots are recovering from the cutting and pegging down. There is no need for the huge mounds that one often sees piled. round carnations that have been layered. ' If before layering is started the surface soil is friable, and can be well loosened, only a little fresh material need be added. After the shoot has been cut and pegged down the ,merest cov- ering suffices. Of course, it is unwise to com- mence layering until the shoots are of sufficient length and firmness, but, as a rule, they will be found quite fit by now, when an effort should be made to get the work done as soon as pos- sible, for the loss of a week may have disas- trous results later on if the autumn should turn out to be cold and wet.—" Wick,' in `!Farm and Home?)

div.head: Palace and Hippodrome.
div.p: Palace and Hippodrome.

One is inclined to think of an opium den as .the resort of inert individuals. Josh Clifton and the Six C,eylons make it one of the 'live- liest spOts on earth. They appear to enjoy falling from heights and indulging in wild acrobatic performances. A diminutive member of the company creates great amusement. Dressed as a ballet girl, hiai figure is quite a treat.

But the palm for fun-making 'must be given this week to Gus- Garrick. His remark that while "a horse may be driven to the water; a pencil must be led," seems a little strange at first; but it is quite true, unless it happens to be a slate pencil. His make-up as a Swiss !Shepherdess was quite breezy and caused roars of laughter.

;Miss Madge Clifton ,is as charming and muscular as ever. Her rounded form is far from suggesting such Vstonishing physical powers as she -possesses. The Zylbastrians are accomplished harpists and performers on in- struments fashioned on the dulcimer principle, but producing great effect in harmony. The Murattis—quite a popular pair in the halls— portrayed the latest Continental dances; and Leslie Carter was very entertaining at the piano. Willie Robbins, American 'comedian And eccentric dancer, completed an admirable arrly of talent.

The Hippodrome pictures should. not be' over- looked. - This week there is a splendid film showing our artillery in action. presents in graphic detail the arduous any: •tre,r_tendo as work of this branch of the service. This re- markable picture is most absorbing. ,

div.head: Money.
div.p: Money.
ROUND OF FESTIVITIES FOR THE BATTALION.

There was great enthusiasm in Warrington on Tuesday afternoon when a large contingent of the men of the South Lancashire Regiment arrived home from the South of England on a short leave. At first it was announced that they were com- ing in at six o'clock and that they wmild be received by his Worship the Mayor on behalf of the citizens, but the original intentions were altered: However, the exact hour of arrival— about three o'clock—appears to have leaked out, as by that time the •approaches to Bank Quay ,Station were thronged with people— mostly women and children, the latter anxiously waiting to see "daddy." Large numbers , were also collected „ along Sankey- street and in, front of the Town' . The sound of a bugle announced the arrival of the train, and about fifteen minutes later the men were lined up along Parker-street. They looked exceedingly well -after their extended training and carried full marching kit, with the exception of rifles and great coats. They. were under the 'command of Major Robson J. Choiley, with Major W. McClure, Captain T. D. Killick, Lieut. Clarkson, Lieut. A. E. Newton and Regimental Sergeant-Major Russell. Headed r)-. their own Bugle Band (Sergeant-Drummer Ellison in charge) .the.men Marched 'aria Parker- street, Sankey-street, Legh-street and Bath- street to the Drill Hall. Although -there was no vigorous cheering along the route—there are not many vigorous young lungs available at three o'clock in the afternoon—there .was .much general enthusiasm and the large force of police and special constables on duty had a busy time preventing anxious friends; from breaking the ranks.
meats of the Warrington boys with deep inter- est': He knew they would perform their more serious duties the same as they had done whilst they had been in training. (Cheers.)

div.head: WELL-CONDUCTED BATTALION.
div.p: A WELL-CONDUCTED BATTALION.
Arrived at the DrillJall, the men were paraded in the building, and, previous to dis- missing them,
Major Chorley said be would like to thank them for the way they had behaved. themselves. He d/id not think any body of men could have behaved better.

Proceeding, he detailed the arrangements kindly made for their entertainment by Capt. Mathams. and the 'people of WaiTington. "One word' more," concluded Major Chorley, "I am not going to keep you here talking. On Sunday you will fall-in here at 4.30. I want you to play the game properly and turn up. There must be no such thing as over-staying your leave because you are pressed to do so by your friends. You have, played the game up to now, and I want you to play the game until you come hack." The battalion was then dismissed, and the men, breakinl off singly; or in small groups, went home with their wives and families or friends.
