div.p: ENTERTAINMENT IN THE
HIPPODROME.

There were three cheers given for Mr. W. A. Jackson, manager of the Palace and Hippo- drome, for the splendid programme arranged for Wednesday afternoon's entertainment, and for Captain Mathams and the committee who worked so well in connection with the reception of the men of. the South Lancs. Out- side the theatre, kindly lent by Mr. Frank Macnaghten and the directors, was a great dis- play of flags and bunting, and the inside of the building was also beatitifull,y decorated with flowers and foliage. A very large nuniber of the Battalion applied for tickets. The stalls were reserved for officers and non-commissioned officers, and the whole floor of the theatre was occupiekl by tile last-named and their families. His Worship the Mayor and some prominent citizens were present. , The galleries were crowded with the men and their families, and many an infantile_ chorus was raised during the progress of the programme. Several Navy lads on leave and a number of wounded men were amongst the audience. A great feature of the afternoon, was the Band of 'the Reserve Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, under the leadership of Mr. Ernest A. Widdop, bandmaster, a popular and clever musician, who formerly wielded the baton in the. Hippodrome orchestra He had a special welcome; and certainly the band of the regi- ment has made rapid strides since he took up his present position. This was evidenced on Wednesday when they performed "Reminis2 cences of Grieg h. (Godfrey), a lengthy' work requiring exceptional skill and unanimity. The augmented orchestra of the theatre, under Mr. T. H. 'Halley, was in fine form, and, gave an enlivening selection, a rag-time "Smash up," in rattling style. All the artistes on the Palace and Hippodrome kindly gave their services. We had Leslie Carter, entertainer at the piano; the Murattis, whirlwind dancers; Maggie Clif- ton and her partner, in- their wonderful equili- bristic performance; 'Josh Clifton and his six CeylonS; in "Fun in an Opium Den"; Willie Robbins, comedian and dancer; the Zylbas- trials, musical novelty; and, above all, Gus garrick, who was excruciatingly funny. He was in great form 'and rose to the occasion. His appearance as a Swiss 'shepherdess evoked screams' of laughter. An admirable item on the programme was the appearance (by kind per- -mission of the management of the Hippodrome, St. Helens) of Archie Pitt, Mona Frewer and Gracie Fields, in 'amusing excerpts from the revue, "It's a Bargain." Miss Fields gave some impersonations, and Gus Garrick also lent a hand. Boxes of cigarettes were distributed.

div.head: ANOTHER FIRM'S WORKMAN.
div.p: ANOTHER FIRM'S WORKMAN.
Lymm Company FinPci Under Munitions Act.

A sitting of :ite General MUnitions Court for the NorthLWestern, District was held Yesterday in the Warrington County Court. Mr. A. J. Ashton, K.C., presided. One Lymm firm complained' that another Lymm firm had infringed the provisions of the Munitions of War Act, 1915-16, by having on-or about' sth July, 1916,, given employment 'to a workman of complainants', named Alfred Pilkington, who had left their employment without giving notice or receiving his certificate. Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, represented cora- Plainante, and Mr. Harry Kay, solicitor, Alan- Chester, appeared for the defendant firm. Prom Mr. Steel's statement it 4peared that the ' young man came ihto their employment on •the , 23rd July, 1915, as a "grinder," and was . given, a badge in Desember. On the morning of the 4th July lasf something was said to him about his work, and he stayed ..,ut after dinner.. Next

morning it was found that.Pilkington was work- ing for the other 'Company.. Mr. Steel wrote on the 6th.of July to the firm, informing them of the fact that Pilkington had been working for complainanis, and that he had been asked to return to his employment. Defend- ants replied that the young man was thgir workman, having come to them before the lirar commenced, and that When he becalm:. skilled the complainant's got hold of,him.. He had left them without asking for his certificate or even k getting his insurance card. Mr. Steel went on to say that the complainants wer, engaged on contracts directly or indirect- with the Government.,
Mr. Kay, in cros•;-examining, suggested that the complainants had taken not only Pilk- ington but also twelve men duriing the past year from hill 3" clients. -

The Chairman said if , that were so he could bring a • cross summons, but it was not an\ answer to the present case. He intimated that he would 'hold that the yoUng man was nroperly employed by the complainants on the date mentioned. A fine of £1 was imposed and an order made for payment of a guinea costs. . 'Mr. Kay expressed the intention of his clients to proceed with reference to the men which they alleged had been taken from them by the complainant company.

div.head: COLONEL DUTTON FAIRCLOUGH'S REGRET.
div.p: COLONEL DUTTON FAIRCLOUGH'S REGRET.

Colonel button lairclough, who, was also warmly cheered, said it was his pleasing duty to propose a vote of thanks to • the directors of the theatre and Mr. Jackson, also to the artistes who had come and given them that entertain- ment. .He was sure they were all very •pleased .at the Way in Which they had been entertained. (Cheers.) He also included the staff and the committee who had given the cigarettes, and also everyone who had helped at the entertain- ment. (Applause.) It had been a pleasure to him to be there to meet them. It was a bitter disappointment when he received the news from. the Medical Board at Sandwich and was obliged to give up the command of the Battalion (the Colonel had not been passed for foreign service); but he would follow their movements wherever they might be at home or abroad. (Cheers.) They did not know what was going.to happen, but he hoped they would be. able to: drive the. Germans black into their own country, and he was sure the welcome they would receive when they came back to Warrington would compen- sate for any hardship they might have under- gone. - (Cheers.) The vote of thanks was heartily passed, and the Mayor read a telegram from Colonel Gordon Roberts conveying his best wishes to the Battalion. Colonel Roberts was formerly in the Territorials, and is now in the Lancashire Fusiliers.•
The band then played "God bless the Prince of Wales and "God save the King,'' terminat- ing a most •enjoyable afternoon.

Various sentiments were thrown on the screen —"The Battalion will enjoy itself," "Three cheers for Colonel Dutton Fairclough," "Don't be bite at the dance to-nigl)t," "Jolly good luck to Mr. Jackson and the artistes and staff," all of which were duly apPreciated. .Finally ap- peared, "Directors, managers, artistes and staff wish you good luck."

div.head: IMNCE IN THE PARR HALL.
div.p: IMNCE IN THE PARR HALL.
A Lame Company Have An Enjoyable Evening.

Any number near six hundred might be applied to the joyous company which assembled in Parr Hall from eight o'clock onward on Wednesday night. It was a brave show, and (lancing was continued spiritedly until an early hour next morning to the music of the fine band of the Reserve Battalion South Lancs., Mr. E. A. Widdop, conductor. This band cer- tainly rendered splendid services ,on Wednes- day, appearing at the Hippodrome, in the after- noon and supplying :a ball programme of twenty items and several extras at night. Here is the list:—

Waltz, "Nights of Gladness ; two-step, "Police- man's Holiday "; lancers, "Sharps and Flats " ; barn dance, "Coon's Holiday "; veleta, " Mirama" ; lancers, " Sousa "; two-step, "Blaze Away " •' waltz, "Meet Me To-night "; two-step, " Noisy Ned " ; lancers, "Revues of London "; doris waltz, " Un Pen D'Amour "; two-step, "Colonel Bogey "; lancers, "Grand March "; waltz, "Destiny " ; two- step, "Steadfast and True "; .waltz, "Girl in the Taxi "; barn dance "Jovial Darkness "; lancers, " Time of My Life "; schottische, "Revels "; waltz, "Costume Ball."

The none too easy duties of M.C.'s were suc- cessfully undertaken by Sergeant-Major Morris, Company-Quartermaster-Sergeant Coakley and Sergeant Goodwin. Everyone was delighted with the way in which the hall was decorated by Messrs. Peter Walker .and Son. Around the cornice and bal- cony were cordons of flags and streamers and handsome shield trophies were placed at inter- vals on the walls. Over the platform, where the band performed their pleasing task, was suspended a hiige Union Jack, flanked on either side with the flags of our Allies, and above was a large scroll with the words—rather prophetic as it happened-- " WOlcome North; Forget the Zepps and mind your steps." _ _

Facing the platform was an incitement to "To-night's the night." The Parr Hall was kindly lent for the oecasion by the Mayor and Corporation, and they also supplied a number of decorative plants. The refreshment buffets occupied the con- stant attention of large number of willing helpers, and this important department was under the able direction of Mrs. Brereton Fair- dough, president, • and members of the Ladi2s' Territorial Equipment Fund Committee. Amongst those present were: His Worship the Mayor, Lieut.-Colonel Brereton Fairclough and Brereton Fairclough, Lieut.-Colonel Dutton Fairclough and Mrs. J. D. Fairclough, Mrs. Gordon Roberts, Mrs. R. Johnson, the Misses Johnson, Captain MathamS and Mrs. Mathams, Major R. J. Chorley, Major W. McClure, Captain T. D. Killiok, Lieut. Clark- son, Lieut. A. E. Newton, Captain R. D. Fair- dough, Colonel Moeatta, Captain McPhail, Lieut. McPhail, Reg,imental-Sergeant-Major Russell and Mrs. Russell.

A warning whistle about ten o'clock brought the.company to attention, and . Major Chorley, officer commanding, expressed the thanks of those present to the Mayor and Corporation and all concerned' far the trouble which had been taken on behalf of the men -of the Battalion. They had also to thank the band for their excellent music. (Cheers.) His - His Warship the Mayo': said that when Captain Mathams saw him and told him the battalion was coming home and asked him what they could do, without consulting the Corpora- tion or committees, he placed the Parr Hall at their disposal. What he had done in this case he would do in the future, because he knew that if the cause was a worthy one the people Of Warrington would back him up. (Laughter and cheers.) Those who had the good fortune to be present on Wednesday night will , long emember a happy experience.
